subject: history
title: Early India & China
objective: Keep the Asian histories on the same map

lesson.opening: How do texts, archaeology, and later traditions give us different access to early societies?

sections.heading: The institutional thread
sections.body:
Urban settlement and changing centers of population

Religious traditions and social orders

Political consolidation in China

sections.heading: A model to test
sections.body: Preserve separate regional sequences. The Vedic traditions do not supply a complete account of the earlier Indus cities. Texts, inscriptions, and archaeology have different strengths and limits.

sections.heading: Keep the question
sections.body: How do texts, archaeology, and later traditions give us different access to early societies?

activities.prompt: Which happened first: “Mature Indus cities” or “Qin unification”?
activities.hint: Compare the dates on the unit timeline.

activities.prompt: “Two populations speaking related languages must be a single biological race.” — is that an event claim or an interpretation?
activities.hint: Language relationship alone does not establish a biological population, still less a hierarchy of ability.

activities.prompt: Put these events back in chronological order.
Place the Indus, Ganges, and Yellow River on the map. Do not collapse them into one setting.
activities.instructions: A few sentences are enough. Cite a passage when it helps.
